title: Is "posh" really an acronym? | WORD MYTHS

entries.note: Formed from [[from:bunk]], with de- here acting as an intensifier rather than meaning down or away, so it means complete nonsense.
An obsolete American English word for nonsense, short for [[from:bunkum]]; an orphaned negative that [[gave:debunk]].
Means nonsense; a misspelling of [[from:Buncombe County]], to which a North Carolina politician addressed a long, boring speech in Congress in 1820.
North Carolina county addressed in an 1820 congressional speech; its misspelled name gave [[gave:bunkum]].
Not from [[unrelated:port out, starboard home]]; perhaps from slang posh for a coin or halfpenny, posh meaning a dandy, or Urdu [[from?:safed posh]], dressed in white.
The false acronym behind [[see:posh]], supposedly stamped on tickets for the coolest cabins on Britain–India voyages; no such ticket has ever been found.
Acronyms weren't common in English until about the mid-1800s, popularised by business and technology, so many supposed acronyms are false; such myths often skew nautical.
Thoroughly Germanic, from the Old English word for feces; not an acronym of [[unrelated:ship high in transit]].
False acronym for [[see:shit]], claiming manure was stored on higher decks to keep it dry; the myth is far younger than the word.
Not an acronym of [[unrelated:to insure promptness]]; origin uncertain, probably from tipping or tapping something, like a coin, towards someone.
False expansion of [[see:tip]]; Rob once objected it should spell TEP, though [[see:ensure]] and [[see:insure]] are etymologically the same word.
Etymologically the same word as [[same-root:insure]], noted while debunking [[see:to insure promptness]].
Etymologically the same word as [[same-root:ensure]], noted while debunking [[see:to insure promptness]].
The game's name is sometimes said to stand for [[unrelated:touch and go]], but it is probably just a word for tapping people.
A satisfyingly apt but false expansion of [[see:tag (game)]].
Not short for [[unrelated:save our souls]] or [[unrelated:save our ships]]; chosen because it is quick and clear in Morse code.
A shoehorned false expansion of [[see:SOS]].
Another false expansion of [[see:SOS]], which Rob finds better, though distress calls aren't necessarily from ships or about several of them.
An earlier radio distress call, not short for [[unrelated:come quickly distress]]; it is [[from:CQ]] plus D for distress.
A rumoured but false expansion of [[see:CQD]].
A general radio call to ships and land stations, not a summons for help; adding D gave [[gave:CQD]].
Simply means new things, like the earlier French [[see:nouvelles]]; not an acronym of [[unrelated:notable events, weather and sports]] or [[unrelated:north, east, south and west]].
Just paper with news on it, not an acronym of [[unrelated:north east west south past and present event report]], a claim seen on TikTok.
Earlier French term meaning new things, used in much the same way as [[see:news]].
A false acronymic explanation of [[see:news]].
Another false acronymic explanation of [[see:news]].

entries.term: north east west south past and present event report
entries.note: A hilariously inaccurate false acronym claimed to explain [[see:newspaper]].
An expansion invented after the word exists; it can mean false folk acronyms or deliberately created ones like [[see:CARE]] or the [[see:USA PATRIOT Act]].
Blamed for the false story, put in one of his books, that [[see:cabal]] is an acronym.
Not an acronym of five plotters against Charles II (Clifford, Arlington, Buckingham, Ashley, Lauderdale); probably from Hebrew [[from:kabbalah]], received law.
First used in 1945 for aid sent to Europe after World War II under [[from:CARE]]; the collocation was rare before that.
Originally the Cooperative for American Remittances to Europe, later recast as Cooperative for Assistance and Relief Everywhere to keep the acronym; gave [[gave:care package]].
Rob's favourite elegant if stretched [[see:backronym]], though he objects to the A in USA standing for America.
The US Geological Survey's Biodiversity Information Serving Our Nation's Species, a species-tracking programme, praised as an apt [[see:backronym]].
Not inspired by [[unrelated:Thomas Crapper]]; it became American slang, coined mostly by college students, shortly after his time.
Victorian London plumber and toilet manufacturer whose name coincidentally matches [[unrelated:crap]]; his patents were for plumbing parts, not the toilet.
An Americanism, not derived from [[unrelated:Thomas Crapper]], though company publicity helped spread that false etymology.
Not an acronym of [[unrelated:unlawful carnal knowledge]] or [[unrelated:fornication under consent of the king]]; Germanic, perhaps from words for striking, pushing or fidgeting.
False acronym for [[see:fuck]]; when that word was first recorded, [[see:knowledge]] was spelled cnawlece.
Spelled cnawlece when [[see:fuck]] was first recorded, undermining the [[see:unlawful carnal knowledge]] myth.

entries.term: fornication under consent of the king
entries.note: False acronym for [[see:fuck]], claiming couples needed royal permission; [[see:king]] was then spelled cyning and [[see:fornication]] came later.
Spelled cyning at the time, so it can't have supplied the K in the [[see:fornication under consent of the king]] myth.
Recorded in English later than [[see:fuck]], probably brought by the French, so it can't underlie that word.
False story tying [[see:fuck]] to English archers at [[see:Battle of Agincourt]] taunting the French that they could still pluck yew bows.
The 1415 battle where the French supposedly cut off English archers' fingers, setting for the [[see:pluck yew]] and [[see:two fingers]] stories.
The British rude gesture with index and middle fingers, the one actually linked to the Agincourt archer story rather than the middle finger.
The Latin name for the rude finger gesture, meaning the impudent or indecent finger.
Not a spoonerism of [[unrelated:flutter by]]; an Old English word with Germanic cognates like Dutch [[same-root:botervlieg]].
A charming but false claim that [[see:butterfly]] is its spoonerism.
Dutch word for the butterfly, comparable to English [[same-root:butterfly]]; one of many Dutch names for the insect.
One of the old Dutch names for the butterfly, alongside [[see:butter witch]] and [[see:butter shite]].
Another old Dutch name for the butterfly.
Old Dutch name for the butterfly, either because they supposedly ate butter off windowsills or because their yellow excrement looks like butter.
Not short for [[unrelated:shortened language]]; probably from older slang like [[from?:sling the jaw]], perhaps linked to a Nordic phrase about abusing with words.
A myth about [[see:slang]] with no historical support; slang terms like [[see:raspberry tart]] aren't necessarily shorter, and some like [[see:chuegy]] shorten nothing.
Cockney rhyming slang for fart, cited to show [[see:slang]] isn't necessarily shorter than what it replaces.
Short-lived Gen Z term, supposedly coined by a student in 2013, for slightly off-trend people, especially millennials; a shortening of nothing.
Older slang that [[gave?:slang]] may have come from.
Generally taken as short for [[from:charisma]], though the YouTuber who coined it says it wasn't specifically inspired by that word.
Briefly used in 19th-century American English for someone using abusive language or a ranting partisan; the hosts want it revived for elections.
When a word changes to fit a false idea of its origin, as with [[see:cockroach]] or [[see:asparagus]]; common with animals and plants.
From Spanish [[from:cucaracha]], reshaped by English speakers into cock plus roach, a simple [[see:folk etymology]].
From Telugu, a language unfamiliar to English speakers; it absorbed the spelling of goose despite having nothing to do with geese.
Most likely from French [[from:coquetier]], an egg cup in which Sazerac cocktails were first served in New Orleans.
Once reshaped into [[see:sparrowgrass]] by speakers puzzled by the Latin, before a concerted effort restored the original spelling.
Former English name for [[see:asparagus]], from sparrow and grass because it looks grass-like; Jess wishes it were still used.
The German word for [[see:asparagus]], everywhere in Germany when the season begins.
Nothing to do with out or rage; from Latin [[from:ultra]], excess, via Old French [[from:oultrage]], misread by English speakers as out plus rage.
Shows the excess sense of [[see:outrage]]: an outrageous outfit is excessive, not enraging.
Blamed for the vowel change in [[see:outrage]] and for many of English's problems.
Neither from Jerusalem nor an artichoke; a sunflower root, with Jerusalem from Italian [[from:girasole]], sunflower.
From Italian [[from:articiocco]] and French [[from:artichaut]], perhaps conflated with chaud; sometimes hearty choke, choke perhaps from its choking heart or invasiveness.
From Old English [[from:wermod]], unrelated to worm or wood, perhaps man plus courage; possibly influenced by its use repelling larvae, insects and hawks' mites.
Really just a long chair; Rob has heard it as chaise lounge, only on American television, a fairly modern bit of sense-making.
Has nothing to do with axe: Middle English picas, from Latin [[from:picus]], woodpecker, its blade shaped like a woodpecker's beak.
